title: Blanca Well Depth and Drilling Cost Guide
meta_description: Blanca wells have a 102-foot median depth, with typical finished-well costs of $11,100-$19,600.
h1: What Blanca Wells Cost, Produce, and Require
intro_html:
For land and homes around Blanca, the well records point to generally moderate depths and solid reported production. The median completed well is 102 feet deep, and the middle half runs from 55 to 160 feet. Reported yields are also favorable, with a 12.0 gallons-per-minute median among wells that list a pump yield.

That does not make every parcel predictable. The records include wells as deep as 820 feet, and most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. Before buying, compare nearby well permits, confirm the existing well’s construction and testing, and price the site work that goes with a new water system.

sections.heading: Blanca well depth depends on the local ground
sections.html:
Blanca’s recorded well depth is moderate by local standards: the median is 102 feet, while the middle half falls between 55 and 160 feet. Forty-one percent of recorded depths are under 100 feet, and 55% are between 100 and 300 feet. Only 4% fall between 300 and 600 feet, with no recorded wells at 600 feet or more in that depth mix.

The deepest record is still 820 feet, so a nearby shallow well is not a guarantee for a new location. Mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground helps explain why bids can vary from parcel to parcel. For a driller, the 55-to-160-foot middle range is a useful planning bracket, but the bid should account for the chance that actual conditions differ.

sections.heading: What a Blanca well may produce
sections.html:
Among the 137 permitted wells that report a pump yield, the median is 12.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Fifty-three percent report yields from 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 44% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Four percent report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, while 0% are listed under 1 gallon per minute.

Those figures are encouraging for ordinary household planning, but they are not a promise for an untested well. Yield records are available for only part of the permitted set. Ask for the well completion report and a current production or recovery test. Irrigation, livestock, and additional buildings can require a different water-rights review than a household well.

sections.heading: Blanca water levels and the recorded trend
sections.html:
Static water level means the depth from the ground surface down to standing water when the well is not being pumped. In Blanca-area records, the median static water level is 45 feet, with the middle half between 28 and 70 feet. That gives a reasonable expectation for pump planning, but the measurement is tied to the individual well and the date it was measured.

The decade figures do not show a simple decline in the recorded water table. The median depth to water was 65 feet in the 2010s and 43 feet in the 2020s, meaning the later recorded group was closer to the surface. That comparison is not a continuous monitoring record, so it should not replace a current measurement on the property.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Blanca, and when
sections.html:
Colorado Division of Water Resources permit records show 697 wells within the mapped area, with 470 recorded as constructed. The most represented drillers are Heersink Drilling, also listed as Heersink, Scott, with 61 records; Mitchell Drilling Co., listed as Mitchell Jr., John C., with 27; and Rocky Mountain Waterworks LLC, listed as Phythian, Donald L., with 27.

Permit activity spans the 1950s through the newest permit year, 2025. The busiest decades in the records were the 2000s with 122 permits, the 2010s with 123, and the 2020s with 120. A permit is useful history, not proof that an old well still works. Match the permit to the property and inspect the current pump, casing, grout, and electrical system.

sections.heading: New-well drilling cost around Blanca
sections.html:
The cost model for Blanca assumes mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground and a drilling rate of $50 to $75 per foot. At the 102-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $5,100 to $7,600. That is only the hole, not a working water system.

A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $11,100 to $19,600 at the median depth. A deeper-than-typical hole can move the price higher, as can difficult access, casing or grout requirements, power distance, and site conditions. Treat the model as a budgeting range for a bid, not a fixed quote. Get the driller to state what is included and what happens if the hole is dry or needs additional depth.

sections.heading: Blanca risks to check before construction
sections.html:
The mapped area includes 5 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 6 historic mine features within about 10 miles. There are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in that search area, but that does not establish that every private well is safe. Test an existing well before relying on it, and ask a qualified water professional which tests fit the parcel and its surroundings.

Low yield is not the leading pattern in the available yield records, but dry holes and poor production remain possible at a new location. Check the permit, construction report, casing and grout, pump test, and water quality history. Septic setbacks, soil, driveway access, electrical service, and the home’s building site also need to be reviewed before drilling or finalizing a house plan.

sections.heading: Buying or building near Blanca, Fort Garland, or San Luis
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, not a countywide assumption. Search neighboring permits around the property and compare depths, yields, water levels, aquifer descriptions, and construction dates. Records identify 663 wells with an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, 17 with the Unconfined San Luis Vall aquifer, and 6 with the Unconfined San Luis Valley Aquifer. No recorded wells are identified in the Denver Basin aquifer.

For an existing home, make the sale contingent on reviewing the well permit, production, water quality, and equipment. For a vacant lot, obtain a site-specific drilling proposal and confirm the DWR permit path before excavation. Conditions near Fort Garland, San Acacio, San Luis, Alamosa East, Alamosa, and Mosca may help with regional comparison, but they do not replace evidence from the immediate parcel.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Blanca, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth near Blanca is 102 feet. The middle half of wells ranges from 55 to 160 feet, while 41% are under 100 feet and 55% fall between 100 and 300 feet. The deepest record is 820 feet, so a nearby shallow well should not be treated as a guarantee for a new parcel.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Blanca?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $75 per foot in mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 102-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $5,100 to $7,600. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $11,100 to $19,600. Actual bids depend on depth and site conditions.

faq.q: How much water do Blanca wells produce?
faq.a: Among 137 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 12.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Fifty-three percent report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 44% report more than 15. These are recorded results, not a guarantee for an untested well.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Blanca?
faq.a: The permit map shows 5 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 6 historic mine features within about 10 miles, with 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those figures do not prove a specific well is safe or unsafe. Test the property’s water before drinking it, and review its construction and prior testing.

faq.q: Can I build a house on a lot near Blanca with a well?
faq.a: A buildable lot needs more than a nearby well record. Confirm the DWR permit path, compare neighboring wells, and check the parcel’s water quality, expected yield, septic conditions, access, electrical service, and building layout. Domestic or household use accounts for 56% of recorded permits, but the permitted use of the specific property controls.
